slides: Open the chapter as the point where large-sample statistics becomes local geometry. The data cloud shrinks at rate one over square-root sample size, so the first question is which tangent and normal directions determine efficient return from the observed statistic to the statistical model.

Use the route slide to separate first-order and higher-order thinking. Full exponential families are easy because the observed sufficient statistic is already a model coordinate. Curved families need a return map, ancillary fibers encode that return map, and curvature explains what first-order efficiency cannot see.

The observed-point cloud makes asymptotics visible without formulas first. In expectation coordinates the MLE in a full exponential family matches the observed statistic, so the ellipse simply shrinks around the truth. This is the clean benchmark for everything that follows.

A curved exponential family introduces a geometric detour. The observed statistic lives in the ambient flat family and usually misses the curved model. Maximum likelihood becomes a projection back to the curve, and the local normal direction explains first-order Fisher efficiency.

Ancillary fibers are not an optional embellishment; they are the estimator. Every nearby ambient observation is assigned to a model point by lying on some fiber. Consistency asks fibers to pass through the model, while first-order efficiency asks them to meet the model orthogonally.

The Schur-complement slide turns the fiber angle into a covariance calculation. The local coordinates split error into parameter and fiber directions. If the off-diagonal metric block vanishes, the nuisance fiber does not inflate variance; tilted fibers reduce precision and produce a visible penalty.

Higher-order asymptotics begins after the tangent approximation has already done its job. Bias correction removes the leading drift, then remaining covariance differences can be organized by curvature terms: model curvature, coordinate curvature, and estimator-dependent ancillary curvature.

Use the simulation lab as a sanity check on the theory. Both estimators are locally consistent, but the tilted-fiber estimator has inflated variance because its fibers leak normal noise into the reported parameter. This is Fisher efficiency as a measurable angle condition.

Hypothesis testing uses the same geometry as estimation. A moving boundary for acceptance and rejection behaves like another ancillary family near the null point. First-order agreement among familiar tests comes from tangent geometry, while second-order behavior depends on boundary angle and curvature.

Close by asking students to name the local object before naming the theorem. Is the calculation about an observed point, a projection, a fiber, a Schur complement, or a curvature correction? That habit keeps asymptotic theory grounded in inspectable geometry rather than symbolic bookkeeping.
